newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing debt market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing debt market report.

text.p: Dutch bonds lost territory in nervous trade on Thursday, solemnly following Germany's drop.
Dutch bonds had already slipped late on Wednesday afternoon after failed attempts to overcome resitance at 102.00 in the June bund futures contract induced profit-taking.
Dealers said the fall had also been caused by worries over today's options expiry on LIFFE, and they pointed at reports on Wednesday forecasting strong growth in the U.S.
"I've heard echoes of forecasts of a six percent growth rate in the U.S. next year," one dealer said. All maturities were well down, with trade concentrating on the ten-year segment.
"Sentiment seems to have turned (against the bond market). People started to twaddle on about it this morning and the market is partly a self-fulfilling prophecy," one dealer said.
Another said: "The trust in longer paper has faded somewhat, as there seems to be little potential in it. There are no more factors that could make the market go in the right direction."
An erroneous statement by the Bank of France, saying it raised its intervention rate to 3.20 percent and then correcting it within two minutes, caused some upheaval, dealers said.
"There's a lot of nervousness and a lot of volatility in the market," one dealer said, pointing at the bund future.
Yet the bond market hardly reacted to U.S. weekly jobless claims for the week ended May 17, released at 1430 GMT.
Claims rose to 322,000, slightly below the estimated 324,000 and up from the previous week's downwardly revised 317,000.
But when the Bund future broke the support level of 100.83, the low reached on April 30, the market took another dive.
"Most people are trying to cover themselves, mainly in futures, and are watching their positions," a dealer said.
Dealers are looking forward to Friday's announcement by the Dutch Finance Ministry of a bond issue.
Many players foresee a reopening of the ten-year 5.75 percent benchmark maturing in February 2007, although one dealer mentioned the possibility of reopening the five-year benchmark.
Another said it would not be a bad idea for the ministry's capital markets agent to come with a bond maturing in some 15 or 20 years' time, given current low interest rate levels.
"But it wouldn't be so easy to place that in this market," he added.
